Hopefully the COP31 climate talks in Antakya will conclude positively. They have gone right to the wire. I am full of admiration for those that work through the night to try and rescue a better deal. And the experts and activists fighting for progress. 

But whether governments agree a commitment on fossil fuels or not, these talks reveal a wider and uncomfortable truth for us campaigners.

We have largely failed to build the mass mainstream public pressure needed to win the politics.

As the talks stall where is the popular pressure on political leaders to strike a bold deal? 

Some will argue that climate negotiations are too complex and too removed from everyday life to inspire mass mobilisation. That COP is no longer the right battlefield to focus on. I agree with that in part - but I think that lets us off the hook too easily.

We have to be honest. Despite years of campaigning, we have not built a broad enough movement of public concern that politicians feel compelled to respond to. Yes the public say they care - but this support is "politically soft". And politicians know it. Even in countries like the UK where we have a government committed to action they don’t feel the public is pressing them to be bold. 

Too much energy and resources remains focused on insider influencing, rather than building popular support beyond those already convinced.

Without winning over the mainstream middle, we will never win the politics of climate change.

We need - as many are saying - a new, integrated campaigning approach focussed on 15 or so key countries, including the USA, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, the UK, Indonesia, India and Australia, built around four complimentary campaign approaches:

1. Building popular engagement aimed the moveable middle. Reaching beyond the already converted through popular culture, sport, music and the things people love and care about.
2. Hard-hitting advocacy and mobilisation of activists. Focus on a small number of clear, achievable policy demands, backed by sustained public campaigning and pressure.
3.High level insider influencing - the movement is good at this.
4. A powerful media war room. To react rapidly to events, shape the public debate using AI, seize cultural moments and ride waves of public concern to build momentum for change.

Some of these elements are in play - but not together. They need to work, not as separate campaigns competing for attention and resources.

Perhaps the biggest challenge now is whether climate funders will come together to back this integrated approach at scale in the countries that matter most.

Too much funding remains fragmented across organisations, issues and individual projects. We need a shared strategy, long-term investment and a willingness to do things differently.

We have the talent, creativity and networks to make this happen. The question is whether we have the collective ambition to change course. The risk is in five years the politics might be worse than now, unless we develop this more integrated approach, in key countries.

Without popular pressure, there will never be the political leadership needed to tackle the climate and nature crisis.

Mind your tokens!

That was the single biggest theme I heard this weekend at the Indonesia Software Developer Conference (DSW) 2026 in Jakarta.

Talking to the young developers there, I caught myself flashing back to my university days -  writing C++, Pascal, and learning object-oriented programming. Times have changed, and the tools evolve almost daily.

One takeaway stood out across almost every session: a key KPI for tech and product teams today isn't just shipping fast - it's burning fewer tokens while getting maximum results.

The discussions around practical engineering were sharp:

 📈  Running agentic coding inside heavily regulated financial environments (and asking honestly if it actually makes teams faster) 
 🔌  Inference engineering and how to serve local LLMs securely at scale 
 🟢  Deploying apps directly through MCP and Git without manual server configuration.

On my way home, I remembered how excited we all were back in 2007 about Web 2.0 and the limitless possibilities for businesses and global communication.

AI carries that exact same energy today just moving at ten times the speed.

If you were building in tech during the Web 2.0 wave, how does this moment compare for you?

In just over two weeks, Jakarta will host the 4th Carbon Digital Conference 2026 (CDC 2026), bringing together policymakers, carbon project developers, investors, corporate buyers, and technology providers to explore the future of Indonesia's carbon economy.

For Indonesia's coal, nickel, mineral processing, oil and gas, and other energy-intensive industries, sustainability is increasingly becoming a business imperative.

As global markets demand lower-carbon commodities, greater supply-chain transparency, and credible emissions reductions, companies face growing pressure to reconcile industrial expansion with environmental responsibility.
The challenge is no longer simply about setting sustainability targets. It is about financing and implementing solutions that deliver measurable results.
From CCS and CCUS to carbon accounting, emissions management, forest conservation, and ecosystem restoration, the carbon economy offers opportunities for Indonesia's extractive industries to strengthen their sustainability strategies.

But carbon credits must complement, not replace, direct industrial decarbonization. How can mining and energy companies participate in credible carbon markets? Can carbon finance support conservation and restoration while creating measurable environmental value? And what role can industrial players take in supporting Indonesia's emerging carbon project developers? These questions are increasingly relevant to investment decisions, international competitiveness, and the long-term sustainability of Indonesia's natural resources industries.

With its growing lineup of government officials, industry leaders, and carbon market specialists, CDC 2026 offers an opportunity to connect industrial sustainability commitments with practical solutions and potential business partnerships.

Registered delegates can also use the conference's Business Matching platform to request 60-minute meetings with other participants on 9 December 2026, in a dedicated meeting room provided by the organizers.
For energy and mining companies, this creates opportunities to engage directly with carbon project developers, technology providers, financiers, and potential partners. The future of Indonesia's extractive industries will depend not only on how much they produce, but increasingly on how sustainably they operate.

Grateful to have represented Indonesia at the Seminar on the CEF Certification Guidebook in Da Nang, Vietnam, on 9 October 2026.

My sincere thanks to the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, Ministry of Transportation of the Republic of Indonesia for the nomination, Pak Sayuta S., and to the Japan Transport and Tourism Research Institute (JTTRI) for the kind invitation. The seminar was held alongside the 54th ASEAN Air Transport Working Group Meeting. It brought together civil aviation regulators and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) experts from ASEAN and Japan to discuss feedstock diversification and certification. It is also part of the JAIF-ASEAN CORSIA Eligible Fuels Certification Guidebook project, which Indonesia proposed.

In my session, "Turning Indonesia's SAF Potential into Production, from a Project Developer Perspective," I shared four points:
 ✔️ Indonesia is preparing for its 1% SAF mandate starting in 2027, with a long-term target of 50% by 2060.
 ✔️ Our feedstock base is large and diverse. It includes POME oil, used cooking oil, empty fruit bunch oil and oil palm trunk, and it can support several SAF production technologies.
 ✔️ Regional expertise delivers results. ICAO approved the POME oil default life cycle value of 18.1 gCO₂e/MJ in November 2025. That is almost 80% lower emissions than conventional jet fuel. It came from close collaboration between the Ministry of Transportation, TRIPATRA andIPOSS (Indonesia Palm Oil Strategic Studies). It is encouraging to see Thailand now taking a similar path with C-Heavy Molasses.
 ✔️ We are building on this. Indonesia is working with Japan to add oil palm trunk to the CORSIA positive list, and we plan to submit our empty fruit bunch oil default value study in early 2027.

ASEAN produces most of the world's palm residues, and producing countries understand this data best. POME has shown that experts from our region can build and defend life cycle calculations at ICAO. Let us keep moving forward together, so that local feedstock becomes real SAF production and supports the aviation sector's net zero goal for 2050.

At TRIPATRA, we are proud to support the national and regional SAF roadmap. Together with government, research institutions and international partners, we will keep working to get local feedstocks recognized as CORSIA Eligible Fuels and to turn that recognition into bankable projects.

Thank you to my fellow speakers and participants for the open and valuable discussions. Looking forward to continuing the collaboration.

Understanding Long Investment Horizons and High Compliance Standards in the Abadi Masela Gas Project Ecosystem

Large-scale strategic gas developments in Eastern Indonesia—centered around the Abadi Masela Block ecosystem—operate on a fundamentally different clock and governance standard than conventional mid-sized energy projects. For capital providers, infrastructure developers, EPC partners, and local consortiums looking to participate in the surrounding ecosystem, understanding these realities early prevents costly missteps.

From an investment origination and enterprise risk governance perspective, two defining pillars govern credible participation around Masela: long-term horizon alignment and uncompromising compliance standards.

Six realities shape how serious stakeholders approach opportunities in this ecosystem:

 1. Multi-Year Development & Execution Horizons: Upstream deepwater gas, LNG infrastructure, and regional supporting facilities unfold across multi-year engineering, regulatory, and financing cycles. Entrants expecting rapid transactional turnarounds often misjudge capital pacing and working-capital endurance.

 2. Tier-One Governance, Compliance & ABAC Discipline: International operators, strategic partners, and institutional lenders enforce strict anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABAC), counter-party due diligence, and transparency standards. Informal shortcuts or opaque intermediary structures do not survive institutional screening.

 3. Ecosystem Opportunities Require Commercial Substance: Supporting infrastructure—spanning ports, marine logistics, industrial utilities, housing/services, and downstream gas utilization—must stand on verified demand, realistic phasing, and clear commercial offtake rather than speculative projections.

 4. Schedule Synchronization with Anchor Milestones: Supporting projects around a flagship development succeed only when their permitting, land readiness, and construction timelines are synchronized with anchor project milestones. Moving too early or without confirmed demand creates stranded-asset risk.

 5. Credible Consortium & Counter-Party Readiness: Local and regional sponsors seeking partnerships with global EPCs or institutional investors must demonstrate clean corporate governance, verifiable track records, and clear role boundaries before entering formal discussions.

 6. Constructive Central–Regional Stakeholder Alignment: Projects in Eastern Indonesia require disciplined, compliant coordination across national policy frameworks, regional authorities, and local communities to safeguard long-term social license and execution continuity.

Indonesia has lost 2.9 million hectares of land and vegetations to forest fires in 2026, and the numbers keep on increasing every day. This reality shaped every decision our team made while developing BizdenBize for T3 Vakfı's COP31 Climate Tech Creathon, and I am proud to share that it carried us all the way to the finals in Antalya, where we presented our work.

As Indonesian students studying in Türkiye, we saw a clear parallel between the 2021 Antalya and Muğla wildfires and the forest fires (karhutla) that return to Kalimantan every dry season. Both countries have strong firefighting fleets and satellite monitoring, yet a large share of fires is still started by human activity: around 89% in Türkiye, through negligence, agricultural burning, and tourism pressure. In other words, weather decides whether a fire spreads, but people decide whether it starts, and this is why we chose to focus on prevention rather than reaction.

BizdenBize is a wildfire prevention and early warning platform that works in three stages:
1. Data ingestion. The system draws on NASA FIRMS (VIIRS 375 m active fire detections), Copernicus EFFIS and ERA5-Land weather data, Indonesia's BMKG SPARTAN fire danger data, and all six components of the Fire Weather Index (FFMC, DMC, DC, ISI, BUI, and the FWI itself). It enriches these with human-activity variables from OpenStreetMap, such as distance to roads, farmland edges, power lines, and peat canals, as well as weekend and holiday flags.
2. A biome-weighted risk engine. Because a Mediterranean pine forest and a tropical peatland burn in very different ways, the model weighs its inputs differently for each region. In Türkiye, it prioritizes moisture and dryness indicators (NDMI and vapour pressure deficit, since pine stays green even when it is dangerously dry), FFMC, slope, and wind. In Indonesia, it prioritizes the Drought Code, peat and groundwater conditions, and days since the last rainfall, because peat fires smoulder beneath the surface. These features feed a calibrated gradient boosting model, so that the output is a meaningful probability rather than an arbitrary score.
3. Delivery to the people who need it. The first people to feel the consequences of these disasters are those living in rural villages near forests, and human-caused fires during severe weather can quickly become fatal. For this reason, we translate the model's output into a simple four coloured danger rating, from green to red, accompanied by a daily checklist of what residents should and should not do.

Huge thank you to our team captain, Dafina Fatima (Product Lead and UI/UX Developer), for delivering an outstanding presentation, as well asMuhammad Ahsanul Iman (Physics and Product Design) andAthar Irsan Sanusi (Environmental Engineering and Research) for being such dedicated and inspiring teammates.

I strongly disagree with the "data centre slowdown" narrative of The Straits Times as it's missing the big picture —the underlying#financial and technical fundamentals of the AI build-out remain stronger than ever. 

What looks like a#slowdown from the outside is actually a rapid structural upgrade in how infrastructure is financed, powered, and engineered.

Here is why the AI infrastructure boom is accelerating, not stalling:

1. Balance-Sheet Firepower Overcomes Friction

Hyperscalers aren't slowing down—they are locked in an existential race where under-investing is the biggest risk. With hundreds of billions in annual CapEx backed by fortress balance sheets and sovereign wealth, tech giants can easily absorb higher development costs, longer timelines, and complex permitting without flinching.

2. "Behind-the-Meter" Power Bypasses Grid Bottlenecks: 

Waiting years for public#utility interconnects is becoming obsolete. Developers are increasingly going off-grid—co-locating directly dedicated natural#GasTurbines microgrids, and funding private utility-scale renewables. Power constraints are driving energy innovation, not stopping construction.

3. Next-Gen Cooling Solves the Water Equation:

Legacy data centres relied on heavy evaporative water cooling. Today’s high-density AI clusters are rapidly transitioning to closed-loop#LiquidCooling systems. These architectures dramatically boost thermal efficiency while slashing ongoing water consumption to near zero.

4. Efficiency Gains Multiply Compute per Watt:

Physical square footage is no longer the only metric that matters. Generational leaps in silicon architecture and algorithmic optimization mean we are extracting exponentially more intelligence per megawatt. Even where physical builds take longer, effective compute capacity continues to surge.

5. Capital Simply Flows to Energy-Abundant Hub:

Constraints in saturated legacy markets don't destroy demand—they redistribute it. Capital is flowing aggressively into regions with stranded energy, vast land, and scalable power infrastructure, creating massive new global compute hubs across the#MiddleEast, the #Nordics, and emerging industrial corridors in #India

AI build-out isn't hitting a wall; it's evolving into a more capital-efficient, energy-independent asset class.

From an idea to one of the five finalists of the UN AI for Climate Action Award 2026.

Climate change is already affecting communities through floods, landslides, droughts, and environmental degradation. The question is, how can we use technology to help address these challenges?

A few months ago, our team submitted AI-Moris to the UNFCCC Technology Mechanism's AI for Climate Action (AICA) Award. AI-Moris is an open-source reforestation system that combines AI, satellite imagery, and drone technology to identify degraded areas, select suitable native tree species, and distribute biodegradable seed pods.

I honestly didn't expect where this journey would take us.

Out of421 submissions from 78 countries, AI-Moris was selected as one of the five finalists, representing Indonesia alongside teams from Tanzania, Mali, and Bangladesh.

This journey brought us to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, on October 13–14, where we had the opportunity to present and showcase our solution at the UN AI for Climate Action Forum 2026.

Beyond the recognition, it was a valuable experience to meet other innovators, exchange ideas, and learn how people from different backgrounds are using technology to address climate challenges.

A big thank you to Benedikta Anindya Bernadi andDavin Djayadi, my teammates who made this journey possible; to kak Gemala Yanuarita, our mentor who accompanied us throughout our time in Phnom Penh; and to all the other mentors, staff, and everyone at Apple Developer Institute for AIML @ UC Surabaya for their support along the way.

This has been a memorable journey, and I'm grateful to have been part of it.

Indonesia’s hotel pricing rebounded for a second straight quarter in Q3 2026. The year-on-year picture was more mixed, especially across cities.

Bank Indonesia’s Hotel Price Index reached 109.89 (2017 = 100), up 2.37% from Q2 and down 1.09% from a year earlier. That puts it about 5% below its Q4 2024 peak. The index tracks pricing in the hotel segment of Bank Indonesia’s commercial property survey.

The city figures show why both the index level and its direction matter. Makassar rose 11.63% year on year and Semarang gained 8.15%. Denpasar still had one of the highest index levels at 123.99, even after a 6.19% annual decline. Jakarta reached 100.04 after a 4.06% quarterly rise, with a much smaller 0.33% annual gain. Each city’s index shows movement relative to its own 2017 base.

What this means for capital decisions:
• Owners can test whether stronger pricing is lifting revenue per available room and operating profit. Track achieved room rates, occupancy and channel costs by segment before carrying the Q3 improvement into the 2027 budget.

•Developers should base new room supply on the local pipeline, demand by segment and a realistic opening ramp. A national rebound says little about how quickly a specific project can fill its rooms at the rates in its feasibility study.

•Lenders should stress-test room rates and occupancy together, then check debt-service coverage after allowing for recurring capital expenditure. Size refinancing against cash flow the property can sustain through a softer quarter.

•Investors can use the index to identify markets for deeper diligence. Price each deal on sustainable property cash flow, required renovation spending and comparable transactions.

Indonesia's drilling market is easier to read by client than by contractor.

Last month I mapped the oilfield service companies working here. This sheet narrows the lens to the companies that own and run the rigs, and it names the client on every job. Ten drillers are on one page: where their rigs are working, for whom, and what each can actually deliver here.

The sheet is not a market-share table. The capability scores are my own analytical judgement from public sources, on a 0 to 3 scale, and they describe what each company delivers in Indonesia rather than worldwide.

Where the rigs are. Onshore, Pertamina Drilling runs 58 rigs and had completed 182 wells by the end of September, 90 of them in the Rokan block for PHR, where Great Wall's rigs also work. Elnusa's modular rig drills for Pertamina Hulu Sanga Sanga, and Apexindo keeps a swamp barge and a jack-up busy in the Mahakam delta for PHM. Offshore, the names change. ADES, which absorbed Shelf Drilling, starts a jack-up for PHM in December; its Admarine 502 drilled Prime Natuna's wells this year and goes to Conrad's Mako in 2027 under its consortium with Pertamina Drilling. PV Drilling has two jack-ups on PHE ONWJ, Ventura's semisubmersible drills deep water for Searah, the Eni–Petronas venture, and Seadrill's drillship found Mubadala's Andaman gas.

What the matrix shows. Indonesian firms hold 5 of the 7 market-leading scores, in land rigs, swamp barges, workover and drilling support, and Pertamina's own PDSI and Elnusa hold both top scores for local content and SOE access. Foreign firms lead in two columns only, jack-ups and deepwater floaters, which are the columns the 2026 programme is moving towards: about two-thirds of this year's high-impact exploration wells are in deep water, and no Indonesian driller owns a rig that can reach them.

Why it looks this way. Pertamina is both the largest client and the owner of the largest driller, so much of the land work stays inside the group. Offshore capacity is tight enough that Apexindo, whose own offshore rigs are booked to 2027, now bids new work with chartered rigs, and churn is real: Velesto's four-year Naga 8 contract off East Java ended in July after three of twelve wells.

For drilling engineers and rig managers: with the exploration target rising from 35 wells to 100, where do you expect rig supply to run short first, on land or offshore?

It is about national pride, self-reliance, and the courage to do difficult things and things that make a difference.

Four years later, in 1962, President John F. Kennedy declared:

"We choose to go to the Moon ... not because they are easy, but because they are hard."

Both leaders understood something fundamental.

Great nations are not built by choosing only what is easy. They are built by having the courage to attempt what others consider impossible.

Challenging national projects push our scientists, engineers, industries, institutions, and younger generations to achieve what once seemed beyond their capabilities.

If we only pursue what is easy, safe, and familiar, we will forever remain followers of nations that dared to do more.

Indonesia has the talent, the resources, and the potential. What we need is the collective determination to believe in ourselves and turn that belief into achievement.

Nuclear power is not simply about generating electricity. It is about proving that Indonesia can master one of humanity's most demanding technologies.

That is why I have dedicated much of my professional life to nuclear energy.

BORED PILE FOUNDATIONS: BEYOND DESIGN CALCULATIONS

One important lesson from specialist foundation engineering is that a bored pile should never be evaluated solely by its diameter, depth, or concrete compressive strength.

A successful foundation is the result of three interconnected engineering disciplines:

1. Geotechnical Engineering
Understanding soil stratification, groundwater conditions, shaft friction, end-bearing resistance, pile group interaction, and settlement behavior. A reliable design must reflect actual subsurface conditions, not merely theoretical assumptions.

2. Construction Engineering
Proper drilling methodology, borehole stability, casing installation, slurry management, reinforcement cage positioning, toe cleaning, and tremie concreting are essential to achieving the intended foundation performance.

3. Quality Assurance & Verification
Construction records, concrete quality control, Crosshole Sonic Logging (CSL), integrity testing, and static load testing provide essential evidence of foundation quality and performance.

From an engineering perspective, these requirements are addressed through SNI 8460:2017 and SNI 2847:2019 in Indonesia, alongside internationally recognized references such as ACI 318, AASHTO LRFD, FHWA Drilled Shaft Guidelines, and ASTM testing standards.

However, applying international standards is not simply about following different calculation methods. It is about understanding the engineering principles, design assumptions, construction requirements, and acceptance criteria behind them.

A few lessons worth remembering:

- Theoretical pile capacity does not automatically guarantee actual foundation performance.
- Construction methodology is an integral part of foundation engineering.
- Poor borehole cleaning or uncontrolled tremie concreting can compromise pile integrity.
- Integrity testing and load testing serve different purposes and should not be treated as interchangeable.
- Construction productivity must never come at the expense of engineering quality and safety.

Ultimately, the responsibility of a senior foundation engineer extends beyond approving drawings or monitoring drilling progress.

It is about ensuring that the foundation is properly designed, correctly constructed, and technically verified to perform throughout the intended service life of the structure.

A successful foundation is not measured by how many piles have been installed or how quickly the work has been completed, but by how reliably those piles transfer structural loads into the ground.

The training was delivered byIr. Lukmanul Hakim, IPM, with support from Deri Iryawan. Both shared valuable insights and practical perspectives on how process safety is implemented and managed in real industrial environments.

Throughout the two-day training, I gained valuable knowledge in several key areas:
Process Safety Fundamentals & Management Systems - Understanding the fundamental principles of PSM, its standards, key elements, and the importance of establishing a strong process safety culture.
Process Risk Management & Safety Barriers – Learning about risk identification and management, the Swiss Cheese Model, and the importance of multiple layers of protection in preventing major process incidents.
Asset Integrity & Operational Safety – Exploring asset integrity and reliability, safe work practices, Management of Change (MOC), Operational Readiness, and Pre-Startup Safety Reviews (PSSR).
Inherently Safer Design & Process Engineering – Understanding how safety considerations should be incorporated into process design, including overpressure protection, pressure relief systems, operating and design envelopes, and safe disposal systems.
Incident Prevention & Continuous Improvement – Learning about emergency preparedness, learning from past incidents, process safety audits, behavioral approaches, and the use of Process Safety KPIs to evaluate safety performance.

As a Chemical Engineering student, this experience broadened my understanding of the responsibilities of chemical engineers beyond process design, optimization, and production efficiency. It reminded me thatprocess safety must be an integral consideration throughout the entire lifecycle of a process facility, from design and operation to maintenance and continuous improvement.

Yesterday, three out of four ChatGPT requests failed. Not because of a hack, or a model bug. Because of a database.

On 21 November, OpenAI ran scheduled maintenance on the Postgres service behind its Primary API, the service that handles authentication across the whole stack. Both read replicas failed at the same time. For 211 minutes, failure rates peaked at 75 percent across ChatGPT and the API, paid and free alike.

Here is the part engineers should sit with. The replicas were not a backup. They were load-bearing. Every request path that needed authentication depended on them, so when they went down, everything went down with them.

I build AKSARA, a system that routes citizen complaints for a city government in Indonesia. It runs on PostgreSQL and calls the Gemini API. If my auth database fell over tomorrow, my users would feel it the same way. That is why I keep asking one question about every dependency I add: if this dies, what else dies with it?

Two replicas are not redundancy if they share the same fate. Real redundancy means a failure in one place cannot take the rest down with it.

Have you ever found a single point of failure hiding in your own stack?

Motorcycles have ABS and traction control to help prevent loss of control.
Riders have helmets, airbags, and protective gear to reduce injuries.
But what helps riders control their own behavior before an accident happens?
Impatience. Overconfidence. Distraction.
Human psychology is an essential part of motorcycle safety.
The attached image is an actual frame captured by our rearview mirror-integrated dashcam. It records not only the surrounding traffic but also the rider's own posture and actions.
When riders know their own behavior is continuously recorded, they become more conscious of how they ride.
I have experienced this myself, and we have received similar feedback from many of our customers.
This is not merely a design concept. It is a behavioral change that riders have actually experienced.
The primary purpose of CockpitCam for Motorcycles (tentative name) is to encourage self-restraint before an accident happens.
Recording evidence after an accident is its secondary role.
At Pit Garage Duct Co., Ltd. in Nagoya, Japan, we have developed a unique motorcycle safety solution:
• Rearview mirror-integrated front and rear recording
• Single-wire architecture
• Patented in Japan, the United States, Indonesia, and India
• More than 2,000 units sold in Japan
We are now developing our next-generation platform with SONY IMX307 sensors, built-in GPS, and an OEM-ready internal wiring architecture.
Vehicle technology helps maintain control.
Protective equipment protects the body.
Continuous recording encourages behavioral self-restraint.
These are complementary approaches to motorcycle safety.
Our contribution is to help riders make safer decisions before an accident happens.
Our mission:
Make dashcams a global standard to save lives.

Most offshore hires fail before anyone starts work.

Eight years placing people from Indonesia into Australian businesses, and the thing that decides it has almost nothing to do with which provider you pick.
Five questions worth asking before you sign.

𝟭. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗱?
Most people answer nothing. Someone sat with the new hire for two days, showed them how it works, and hoped. When that person struggles it gets read as an offshore problem. A local hire with the same handover would have struggled the same way.
Treat month one as the month you finally document how you work.

𝟮. 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺?
Contractor, marketplace freelancer, or employed by a real entity. Ask directly and get it in writing.
In 2024 the Fair Work Commission found an offshore worker in the Philippines was an employee of the Australian business that engaged her, not a contractor. 𝗣𝗮𝘀𝗰𝘂𝗮 𝘃 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗹 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗽 [𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟰] 𝗙𝗪𝗖 𝟮𝟲𝟲𝟵. Worth reading before you sign anything.

𝟯. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗹𝗮𝗽 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀?
"They work Australian hours" means little on its own. Get the window. Plenty of providers run 10am to 6:30pm AEST. If you are in trades and your day starts at 7, that is a three hour hole every morning.

𝟰. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁?
Anyone with fifteen people can claim zero turnover. Ask what the number is at their size, and what it was two years ago. A provider with 300 people quoting five percent is telling you more than one with twenty quoting zero.
Including us. We have had no voluntary attrition, and at our size that is not an achievement.

𝟱. 𝗗𝗼 𝗜 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻?
If the answer is "we allocate someone suitable", walk. You are hiring a person.

What would you add? Eight years in and I am still learning what breaks.

Nvidia lost its CEO. Washington is circling Malaysia.

A hyperscaler told me last week: "We're going full speed ahead."

The headlines tell you what happened. My conversations with the people building these data centres tell me what happens next.

What's changed in the last two weeks:

→ The US is looking at new export rules and licensing for Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore
→ Malaysia is weighing a law to monitor data centre operations and GPU use
→ "Know your end user" is now the baseline for everyone in the chain

The hyperscaler's full take:

"We're not worried. We saw this coming one way or the other. The Jensen incident is just the trigger point. We're going full speed ahead with construction."

Some projects will pause while investors wait for clarity. The serious players had already priced this in.

Why are they so confident?

AI demand isn't slowing. There still isn't enough compute, and neoclouds are still chasing capacity.

The real bottleneck is power. The IEA now projects data centre electricity use could double to about 1,000 TWh by 2030, while transformers, cables and copper are already tight.

Even after the Nvidia sell-off, the hard constraint isn't chips. It's megawatts, and the people who can deliver them.

What this means for hiring in Malaysia:

	1.	Companies that keep building now will lock in the best talent while others hesitate
	2.	Power, grid and electrical leaders stay the scarcest people in the market
	3.	Compliance and trade control expertise is now a must-have

I spend my week talking to the hyperscalers, operators and power players behind these sites. I'll keep sharing what I'm hearing that you won't read in the news.

Follow me if you want the view from inside the industry, not just the headlines.

An unexpected invitation turned into a truly meaningful afternoon.

I was invited to join a roundtable book discussion hosted by The Jakarta Post at @jplivespace, bringing together people from different professional and academic backgrounds to share one book that has shaped the way we think about leadership.

The idea was simple: bring a favourite book, share why it matters, and explore the perspectives behind it.

My choice? No hesitation. The Let Them Theory by Mel Robbins. 📚

This book has been my little companion since mid-2025. What started as casual reading gradually became something much more personal — almost a practical guide through a period of significant transitions in my life and career.

Two simple principles, yet incredibly powerful:

LET THEM — Allow people to think, feel, react, and behave the way they choose.

LET ME — Focus on what I can actually control: my responses, choices, decisions, and actions.

For me, this is one of the most valuable leadership lessons: we can allow others to be who they are without losing control of who we are.

One of my favourite reminders from the book is surprisingly simple:

"Smile & say hello to anyone & everyone you pass or meet."

A small reminder that kindness doesn't have to come with emotional investment. You can smile, be gracious, say hello, and still choose not to carry other people's negativity with you.
Or, in my own interpretation: smile, say hello, and let them. You don't have to give everyone access to your energy. 😉

Throughout late 2025 and 2026, this book has helped me navigate different personal and professional dynamics. I am still learning, still practising, and occasionally still reminding myself to LET THEM. 😅

And perhaps that's what leadership development really looks like: not having all the answers, but continuously learning how to lead others without losing yourself in the process.

The discussion itself was wonderfully orchestrated by IbuAninditta Savitry. Such an engaging conversation, enriched by diverse perspectives, experiences, and interpretations of leadership.

And here's another little personal happiness: I've been wanting to become part of a book club for the longest time. Apparently, the universe heard me. Voilá! 🪽

The bonus chapter? An absolutely fascinating mix of people — from PhD students and psychologists to data engineers, doctors, and professionals from various fields. Different worlds, different experiences, yet connected through books and meaningful conversations.

A reminder that learning doesn't stop when we leave the classroom. Sometimes, the most valuable lessons come from simply sitting around a table, listening, sharing, and being curious about how other people see the world.

Already looking forward to the next book session!

Thank you, The Jakarta Post , for such a thoughtful invitation and wonderful hospitality. Great coffee, delicious food, and a beautifully artsy space. Everything was just perfect!
And of course, @jplivespace.

In just over two weeks, Jakarta will host the 4th Carbon Digital Conference 2026 (CDC 2026), bringing together policymakers, carbon project developers, investors, corporate buyers, and technology providers to explore the future of Indonesia's carbon economy.

For Indonesia's coal, nickel, mineral processing, oil and gas, and other energy-intensive industries, sustainability is increasingly becoming a business imperative.

As global markets demand lower-carbon commodities, greater supply-chain transparency, and credible emissions reductions, companies face growing pressure to reconcile industrial expansion with environmental responsibility.
The challenge is no longer simply about setting sustainability targets. It is about financing and implementing solutions that deliver measurable results.
From CCS and CCUS to carbon accounting, emissions management, forest conservation, and ecosystem restoration, the carbon economy offers opportunities for Indonesia's extractive industries to strengthen their sustainability strategies.

But carbon credits must complement, not replace, direct industrial decarbonization. How can mining and energy companies participate in credible carbon markets? Can carbon finance support conservation and restoration while creating measurable environmental value? And what role can industrial players take in supporting Indonesia's emerging carbon project developers? These questions are increasingly relevant to investment decisions, international competitiveness, and the long-term sustainability of Indonesia's natural resources industries.

With its growing lineup of government officials, industry leaders, and carbon market specialists, CDC 2026 offers an opportunity to connect industrial sustainability commitments with practical solutions and potential business partnerships.

Registered delegates can also use the conference's Business Matching platform to request 60-minute meetings with other participants on 9 December 2026, in a dedicated meeting room provided by the organizers.
For energy and mining companies, this creates opportunities to engage directly with carbon project developers, technology providers, financiers, and potential partners. The future of Indonesia's extractive industries will depend not only on how much they produce, but increasingly on how sustainably they operate.

Developers Ship Agents. Agents Stall At Payment.

The agent economy does not stall because the models are weak. It stalls because the infrastructure underneath the models was built for humans with bank accounts, not software with wallets.

A developer can wire an agent to search the web, write code, call an external API, and produce a polished deliverable in under an hour. Adding a payment action to that same agent takes days, requires a business entity, a Stripe account, a bank integration, and a human approval step that defeats the entire purpose of autonomous operation.

That asymmetry is the real bottleneck in AI automation today.

BananaCrystal is built to close it. The architecture is straightforward: fund a wallet with USDC, convert to USDb, swap to any supported token, settle to any recipient in any supported currency. The agent does not wait for a human to approve a wire. The payment clears in seconds, not days.

For developers building automation products for global clients, that settlement speed matters most when the recipient is outside the dollar system. A contractor in Nairobi, a supplier in Jakarta, a service provider in Bogota: these are the real end-points of the agent economy, and ACH and SWIFT were not designed for them.

The three lines of code that give an agent a wallet should be as frictionless as the three lines that give it a tool call. That is the developer experience BananaCrystal is building toward.

I strongly disagree with the "data centre slowdown" narrative of The Straits Times as it's missing the big picture —the underlying#financial and technical fundamentals of the AI build-out remain stronger than ever. 

What looks like a#slowdown from the outside is actually a rapid structural upgrade in how infrastructure is financed, powered, and engineered.

Here is why the AI infrastructure boom is accelerating, not stalling:

1. Balance-Sheet Firepower Overcomes Friction

Hyperscalers aren't slowing down—they are locked in an existential race where under-investing is the biggest risk. With hundreds of billions in annual CapEx backed by fortress balance sheets and sovereign wealth, tech giants can easily absorb higher development costs, longer timelines, and complex permitting without flinching.

2. "Behind-the-Meter" Power Bypasses Grid Bottlenecks: 

Waiting years for public#utility interconnects is becoming obsolete. Developers are increasingly going off-grid—co-locating directly dedicated natural#GasTurbines microgrids, and funding private utility-scale renewables. Power constraints are driving energy innovation, not stopping construction.

3. Next-Gen Cooling Solves the Water Equation:

Legacy data centres relied on heavy evaporative water cooling. Today’s high-density AI clusters are rapidly transitioning to closed-loop#LiquidCooling systems. These architectures dramatically boost thermal efficiency while slashing ongoing water consumption to near zero.

4. Efficiency Gains Multiply Compute per Watt:

Physical square footage is no longer the only metric that matters. Generational leaps in silicon architecture and algorithmic optimization mean we are extracting exponentially more intelligence per megawatt. Even where physical builds take longer, effective compute capacity continues to surge.

5. Capital Simply Flows to Energy-Abundant Hub:

Constraints in saturated legacy markets don't destroy demand—they redistribute it. Capital is flowing aggressively into regions with stranded energy, vast land, and scalable power infrastructure, creating massive new global compute hubs across the#MiddleEast, the #Nordics, and emerging industrial corridors in #India

AI build-out isn't hitting a wall; it's evolving into a more capital-efficient, energy-independent asset class.

Indonesia’s hotel pricing rebounded for a second straight quarter in Q3 2026. The year-on-year picture was more mixed, especially across cities.

Bank Indonesia’s Hotel Price Index reached 109.89 (2017 = 100), up 2.37% from Q2 and down 1.09% from a year earlier. That puts it about 5% below its Q4 2024 peak. The index tracks pricing in the hotel segment of Bank Indonesia’s commercial property survey.

The city figures show why both the index level and its direction matter. Makassar rose 11.63% year on year and Semarang gained 8.15%. Denpasar still had one of the highest index levels at 123.99, even after a 6.19% annual decline. Jakarta reached 100.04 after a 4.06% quarterly rise, with a much smaller 0.33% annual gain. Each city’s index shows movement relative to its own 2017 base.

What this means for capital decisions:
• Owners can test whether stronger pricing is lifting revenue per available room and operating profit. Track achieved room rates, occupancy and channel costs by segment before carrying the Q3 improvement into the 2027 budget.

•Developers should base new room supply on the local pipeline, demand by segment and a realistic opening ramp. A national rebound says little about how quickly a specific project can fill its rooms at the rates in its feasibility study.

•Lenders should stress-test room rates and occupancy together, then check debt-service coverage after allowing for recurring capital expenditure. Size refinancing against cash flow the property can sustain through a softer quarter.

•Investors can use the index to identify markets for deeper diligence. Price each deal on sustainable property cash flow, required renovation spending and comparable transactions.
